content: 1. The systematic review of vaccines and immunization was analyzed using a TRIC framework, as published in Vaccine in 2018 (Volume 36, Pages 2254-2261). 2. Jo CL, Burchett H, Bastías M Campbell P, Gamage D, Henaff L, and colleagues conducted an international expert workshop to explore the use of existing systematic reviews for developing vaccination recommendations. Their findings were published in Vaccine in 2021 (Volume 39, Pages 3103-3110). 3. The WHO Global Advisory Committee on Vaccine Safety provides accessible resources and updates on vaccine safety, with the latest information accessed on March 8, 2024. 4. Tricco AC, Antony J, Zarin W, Strifler L, Ghassemi M, Ivory J, and colleagues conducted a scoping review of rapid review methods, which was published in BMC Medicine in 2015 (Volume 13, Article 224). 5. Garrity C, Gartlehner G, Nussbaumer-Streit B, King VJ, Hamel C, Kamel C, and others from the Cochrane Rapid Reviews Methods Group provided evidence-informed guidance for conducting rapid reviews, as detailed in the Journal of Clinical Epidemiology. 6. Simmonds M, Elliott JH, Synnot A, and Turner T contributed to the development of living systematic reviews, which are discussed in the book Meta-Research: Methods and Protocols, edited by Evangelou E and Veroniki AA, published by Springer US in 2022. 7. Graña C, Ghosn L, Evrenoglou T, Jarde A, Minozzi S, Bergman H, and colleagues evaluated the efficacy and safety of COVID-19 vaccines in a Cochrane Database Systematic Review published in 2022 (CD015477). 8. Den Boon S, Jit M, Brisson M, Medley G, Beutels P, White R, and others developed guidelines for multi-model comparisons of the impact of infectious disease interventions, published in BMC Medicine in 2019 (Volume 17, Article 163). 9. The Market Information for Access to Vaccines (MI4A) initiative provides data on vaccine access and was last accessed on March 8, 2024. 10. The Risk of Bias 2 (RoB 2) tool, developed by Flemyng E, Moore TH, Boutron I, Higgins JPT, Hróbjartsson A, Nejsgaard CH, and others, offers guidance for assessing randomized controlled trials, as published in BMJ Evidence-Based Medicine in 2023. 11. Sterne JAC, Hernán MA, McAleenan A, Reeves BC, and Higgins JPT authored Chapter 25 of the Cochrane Handbook, which provides methods for assessing risk of bias in non-randomized studies. This chapter was updated in February 2022. 12. The ROBINS-I tool, developed in 2016, provides detailed guidance for assessing risk of bias in non-randomized studies. 13. Whiting P, Savović J, Higgins JPT, Caldwell DM, Reeves BC, Shea B, and colleagues introduced the ROBIS tool for assessing risk of bias in systematic reviews, as published in the Journal of Clinical Epidemiology in 2016 (Volume 69, Pages 225-234). 14. Shea BJ, Reeves BC, Wells G, Thuku M, Hamel C, Moran J, and others developed AMSTAR 2, a critical appraisal tool for systematic reviews that include randomized or non-randomized studies of healthcare interventions, published in BMJ in 2017 (Volume 358, Article j4008). 15. Guyatt GH, Oxman AD, Vist GE, Kunz R, Falck-Ytter Y, Alonso-Coello P, and colleagues introduced the GRADE framework for rating the quality of evidence and strength of recommendations, as published in BMJ in 2008 (Volume 336, Page 924). 16. Balshem H, Helfand M, Schünemann HJ, Oxman AD, Kunz R, Brozek J, and others provided GRADE guidelines for rating the quality of evidence, published in the Journal of Clinical Epidemiology in 2011 (Volume 64, Pages 401-406). 17. Schünemann HJ, Cuello C, Akl EA, Mustafa RA, Meerpohl JJ, Thayer K, and others outlined how tools like ROBINS-I should be used to rate the certainty of evidence in non-randomized studies, as published in the Journal of Clinical Epidemiology in 2019 (Volume 111, Pages 105-114). 18. Davies HTO, Crombie IK, and Tavakoli M discussed the potential for odds ratios to mislead, as published in BMJ in 1998 (Volume 316, Page 989). 19. Alonso-Coello P, Schünemann HJ, Moberg J, Brignardello-Petersen R, Akl EA, Davoli M, and others introduced the GRADE Evidence to Decision (EtD) frameworks for making informed healthcare choices, published in BMJ in 2016 (Volume 353, Article i2016). 20. Moberg J, Oxman AD, Rosenbaum S, Schünemann HJ, Guyatt G, Flottorp S, and others developed the GRADE EtD framework for health system and public health decisions, published in Health Research Policy and Systems in 2018 (Volume 16, Article 45). 21. The WHO Immunization Dashboard provides global immunization data and was last accessed on March 8, 2024. 22. Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, supports global immunization efforts and was last accessed on March 8, 2024. 23. Schünemann HJ, Wiercioch W, Brozek J, Etxeandia-Ikobaltzeta I, Mustafa RA, Manja V, and others developed the GRADE-ADOLOPMENT framework for adapting and developing trustworthy recommendations, as published in the Journal of Clinical Epidemiology in 2017 (Volume 81, Pages 101-110). 24. The IA2030 Monitoring & Evaluation Framework outlines strategies for immunization monitoring and was last accessed on March 8, 2024. 25. The WHO Technical Report Series 1004, Annex 9 (2017), provides detailed guidance on vaccine-related declarations of interest and was last accessed on March 8, 2024. 26. The WHO Declaration of Interests form ensures transparency and integrity in expert advisory roles, requiring disclosure of any potential conflicts of interest. Experts must complete and submit this form prior to participation in WHO activities. 27. The form requires disclosure of financial, professional, or other interests related to the subject of the meeting or work, including any interests that could reasonably be perceived to affect objectivity and independence. 28. Experts must promptly inform the WHO Secretariat of any changes to their declared interests before or during the activity. 29. The WHO Secretariat reviews all declarations to determine the relevance and significance of any potential conflicts of interest. 30. If a conflict of interest is deemed significant, the expert may be excluded from participation in the relevant activity. 31. All declared interests and actions taken to manage them will be disclosed to participants and published in resulting reports. 32. If the objectivity of the work is questioned, the contents of the Declaration of Interests form may be disclosed to external parties if deemed necessary by the WHO Director-General. 33. Completing and signing the Declaration of Interests form signifies agreement to these conditions. 34. Experts unwilling to disclose relevant interests may be required to recuse themselves from the activity.
